chapter.name: Early Humans and Beginning of Civilisation

questions.q: The chapter gives another name for the Harappan script found on seals and pottery. What is it?
questions.a: Sindhu lipi

questions.q: Our early ancestors called australopithecines get their name from the words 'australis' and 'pithecus'. What does 'australis' mean?
questions.a: southern

questions.q: Assertion (A): The cuneiform script of the Sumerians and the hieroglyphic script of Egypt mark the beginning of the historical period, about 5000 years ago. Reason (R): Unlike the Harappan script, these two scripts have been deciphered, so their written records can be read and begin the historical period. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: What is biological evolution? Name the early ancestors and the modern humans that it links, as given in the chapter.
questions.a: Biological evolution is the gradual physical and genetic change through which our early ancestors evolved into modern human beings. It links the australopithecines to modern humans, Homo sapiens.
s: Defines it as gradual physical and genetic changes from early ancestors to modern humans
Names australopithecines evolving into Homo sapiens

questions.q: True or False: For the period before writing, the tools and objects people left behind make it easy to understand their thoughts and ideas.
questions.a: False. Fig. 4.3 says that for the period before writing it is generally difficult to understand the thoughts and ideas of people; artefacts show their ways of living, and only after writing does literature give names, events and social, political and cultural life.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: before writing it is generally difficult to know people's thoughts and ideas; artefacts show ways of living, written documents later give names, events and social life

questions.q: Answer in one line each. (a) What period of time does the chapter call the Quaternary Period? (b) To survive changing climate and environment in this period, what did humans develop? (c) According to the chapter, what ability laid the foundation for the emergence of civilisation?
questions.a: (a) The last 26 lakh years, including the present. (b) Tools, techniques and other forms of technology to make use of natural resources. (c) The ability to produce surplus food and material goods.
s: (a) The last 26 lakh years, including the present
(b) Tools, techniques and other technology to use natural resources
(c) The ability to produce surplus food and material goods

questions.q: Asha says, 'Writing began in India only with the Brahmi script, from about 400 BCE.' Vikram says, 'Writing in the subcontinent is much older, but we still know that earlier people mainly from objects.' Using the chapter: (a) Name the earlier writing system of the subcontinent and the objects it is found on. (b) Take the beginning of the historical period, about 5000 years ago, as about 3000 BCE. About how many years before 400 BCE is that? (c) Why do we still understand the Harappans mainly through archaeological evidence? (d) What does the chapter say happened to the Brahmi script under the Emperor Ashoka? (e) Whose statement is better supported? Justify using your answers.
questions.a: (a) The Harappan (Sindhu-Sarasvati) script, also called Sindhu lipi, a pictographic script found on objects such as seals and pottery. (b) 3000 - 400 = about 2,600 years. (c) The Harappan script has not yet been deciphered, so its writings cannot be read and the evidence used is mainly material. (d) It was formalised by the Emperor Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE and by contemporary Iron Age people all over southern India. (e) Vikram's: the Harappan script is one of the earliest known writing systems and flourished around the same time as cuneiform and hieroglyphs, about 2,600 years before Brahmi, so Asha confuses a later script with the beginning of writing; but because it is undeciphered, Vikram is right that the Harappans are still known mainly from objects.
s: (a) Harappan script (Sindhu lipi), pictographic, on seals and pottery
(b) 3000 - 400 = about 2,600 years
(c) The Harappan script is not deciphered, so we rely on archaeological evidence
(d) Brahmi formalised by Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE
(e) Vikram better supported: writing is far older than Brahmi, yet undeciphered, so objects remain the main evidence

questions.q: What does the name Homo habilis mean, as given in the chapter?
questions.a: handy man

questions.q: A team digging in a cave in Southwest Asia finds a skull dated to about 60,000 years ago, lying with Middle Palaeolithic flake tools. Going by the captions of Fig. 4.6, which human ancestor does the find most likely belong to?
questions.a: Homo neanderthalensis

questions.q: Match each human ancestor in Column I with what the captions of Fig. 4.6 say about it in Column II. Column I: 1. Homo habilis  2. Homo erectus  3. Homo neanderthalensis  4. Homo sapiens. Column II: (a) the only human species living on earth today  (b) lived in Europe and Southwest Asia till about 40000 years ago  (c) lived in the Olduvai Gorge, Tanzania and Kenya  (d) lived in the Eastern African Rift Valley 2 million years ago
What is a fossil, and how does a fossil form?
questions.a: A fossil is the preserved remains, traces or impressions of plants, animals or humans from the distant past. It forms when the remains get buried under layers of earth and slowly turn into stone over thousands or millions of years.
s: Fossil: preserved remains, traces or impressions of plants, animals or humans from the distant past
Forms when remains are buried under layers of earth and slowly turn into stone over thousands or millions of years

questions.q: True or False: Homo sapiens evolved in Africa, and the major wave of movement out of Africa around 125,000 years ago is linked with them.
questions.a: True. The chapter says Homo sapiens, modern humans, evolved in Africa around 300,000 years ago, and the major wave of movement out of Africa around 125,000 years ago is associated with early Homo sapiens, who are now spread all over the earth.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: Homo sapiens evolved in Africa about 300,000 years ago and the wave around 125,000 years ago is associated with them

questions.q: (a) Homo sapiens evolved in Africa around 300,000 years ago. For about how many years did they live there before the wave of movement out of Africa around 125,000 years ago? (b) Until about when, and where, did Homo neanderthalensis live? (c) The chapter says Homo sapiens spread over the world between 50000 and 12000 years ago. Use this to show that Homo sapiens and Homo neanderthalensis could have lived at the same time.
questions.a: (a) 300,000 - 125,000 = about 175,000 years. (b) In Europe and Southwest Asia, till about 40000 years ago. (c) Homo sapiens existed from about 300,000 years ago and were spreading over the world from 50000 years ago, while Neanderthals lived till about 40000 years ago, so the two overlapped in time, for example during the 10,000 years from 50000 to 40000 years ago.
s: (b) Europe and Southwest Asia, till about 40000 years ago
(c) Shows the overlap: sapiens spreading from 50000 years ago while Neanderthals lived till 40000 years ago

questions.q: A school museum is setting up a gallery called 'Out of Africa'. Its notes say: our earliest ancestors evolved and lived in Africa and began to move out around 2 million years ago. The first hominin to exit Africa carried stone handaxes and cleavers. Such tools have been found in other parts of Asia and in Europe. Another major wave out of Africa took place around 125,000 years ago. The gallery will also show a fossil skull and a stone tool. (a) Which hominin was the first to exit Africa, according to the chapter? (b) Name the two kinds of stone tool this hominin carried. (c) Why do handaxes found in Asia and Europe count as evidence of a movement out of Africa? (d) Write one thing the fossil skull and one thing the stone tool can each tell visitors about our ancestors.
questions.a: (a) Homo erectus. (b) Handaxes and cleavers. (c) The same tools are found in Africa and beyond it, which indicates their origin in Africa and their dispersion beyond the continent between 2 and 0.5 million years ago. (d) A fossil skull shows the body of an ancestor, such as changes in skull shape and the gradual straightening of the face (Fig. 4.6); a stone tool shows how they lived and worked, such as chopping meat or scraping skin.
s: (a) Homo erectus
(b) Handaxes and cleavers
(c) Same tools in and beyond Africa show their origin in Africa and dispersion out of it
(d) One thing from the fossil (body or skull shape) and one from the tool (how they lived or worked)

questions.q: Attirampakkam, one of the oldest Palaeolithic sites of the Indian subcontinent, is in which present-day state?
questions.a: Tamil Nadu

questions.q: What were the large cutting tools and scrapers of the earliest Palaeolithic sites in India used for?
questions.a: chopping animal meat, digging out tubers, scraping animal skin and cleaving bones for marrow
o: chopping animal meat, digging out tubers, scraping animal skin and cleaving bones for marrow
ploughing fields and cutting ripe wheat and barley at harvest
cutting stone blocks and bricks to build the walls of houses
carving jade and marble into ornaments shaped like birds

questions.q: Read the statements about the periods of early human history in Fig. 4.7. Statement I: The Neolithic saw a shift from hunting-gathering to agriculture and settled life, with polished stone tools. Statement II: The Chalcolithic is marked by mixing copper and tin to make bronze. Statement III: The Mesolithic used microlithic tools and was a transitional phase between hunting-gathering and agriculture. Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I and III only

questions.q: At early Palaeolithic sites such as Attirampakkam and Isampur, (a) name the two kinds of large cutting tools found, and (b) name the two kinds of rock the chapter says the tools were made of.
questions.a: (a) Handaxes and cleavers. (b) Quartzite and limestone.
s: (a) Handaxes and cleavers
(b) Quartzite and limestone

questions.q: A museum guide shows visitors a piece of ostrich eggshell with lines cut into it and a row of tiny stone blades set into a wooden handle. (a) Name the stone tool that was used to engrave such marks on shell or bone. (b) Why were the tiny blades fixed in a handle, and from what kind of rock were such blades made so that they were very sharp?
questions.a: (a) A burin, or engraver. (b) The microblades were fixed in a handle for ease of use; they were made from rocks with a glassy texture, which are very sharp when freshly made.
s: (a) Burin (engraver)
(b) Fixed in a handle for ease of use; made of glassy-textured rock, very sharp when fresh

questions.q: Answer in one line each. (a) What does 'microlithic' mean in Fig. 4.7? (b) Why is the Mesolithic described as a transitional phase? (c) Name the World Heritage Site in Madhya Pradesh that has hundreds of painted rock shelters with Mesolithic and earlier human occupation.
questions.a: (a) The use of tiny stone tools. (b) It lies between the hunting-gathering way of life and agriculture. (c) Bhimbetka.
s: (a) Tiny stone tools
(b) Between hunting-gathering and agriculture
(c) Bhimbetka

questions.q: A student labels three imaginary sites from what was found. Site X, dated to about 1.6 million years ago: handaxes, cleavers and animal fossils; label 'Mesolithic'. Site Y, dated to about 30,000 years ago: microblades, a bow-and-arrow point and stone beads; label 'later Palaeolithic, made by Homo sapiens'. Site Z, dated to about 10,000 years ago: many microliths, bone points and fish bones in a rock shelter; label 'Mesolithic'. (a) Check the label of Site X. (b) Check the label of Site Y. (c) Check the label of Site Z. (d) Which site best fits the time of the first-ever population explosion in human history? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Wrong. Large cutting tools such as handaxes and cleavers with animal fossils, dated like Attirampakkam (1.5-1.7 million years ago), belong to the early Palaeolithic (Old Stone Age); the Mesolithic began only after the climate warmed around 12000 years ago. (b) Right. The bow and arrow, blades and microblades and the first beads of stone, bone and shell are associated with Homo sapiens, who spread over the world between 50000 and 12000 years ago. (c) Right. After about 12000 years ago microlithic tools helped people gather aquatic food, fishing was the mainstay, and caves and rock shelters were often occupied. (d) Site Z: the population explosion came when the warmer climate, from about 12000 years ago, spread forests and grasslands and gave small game, fish and edible wild grains; Site Y is earlier than that and Site X far earlier.
s: (a) X wrong: early Palaeolithic large cutting tools, far older than the Mesolithic
(b) Y right: bow and arrow, microblades and beads linked to Homo sapiens, 50000-12000 years ago
(c) Z right: microliths and fishing after the warming about 12000 years ago
(d) Chooses Z, linking the population explosion to the warmer climate and wider resources after 12000 years ago

questions.q: Name the stone tool or invention from the chapter that early humans would have used for each task, in one line each. (a) Breaking open an animal bone to take out the protein-rich marrow. (b) Cleaning the inside of an animal skin. (c) Giving a thrown projectile a sharp tip so that hunting becomes more efficient. (d) The later invention used to hunt small game animals. (e) Gathering fish and other aquatic food after the climate became warmer about 12000 years ago.
questions.a: (a) A cleaver, used to cleave animal bones. (b) A scraper. (c) A stone point. (d) The bow and arrow. (e) Microlithic (tiny stone) tools.
s: (a) Cleaver (large cutting tool used for cleaving)
(b) Scraper
(c) Stone point on the projectile
(d) Bow and arrow
(e) Microlithic tools

questions.q: Mehrgarh, the oldest Neolithic site of the Indian subcontinent, lies on which river?
questions.a: the Bolan

questions.q: According to the chapter, what was the hallmark of the Neolithic revolution?
questions.a: the domestication of select animals and plants, bringing them under human control
o: the domestication of select animals and plants, bringing them under human control
the invention of writing on clay tablets to keep records of crops
the mixing of copper and tin to make bronze tools and weapons
the first painting of cave walls and the making of beads

questions.q: Assertion (A): By about 4000 BCE, the people of Mehrgarh had become popularly known as the Chalcolithic people. Reason (R): The people of Mehrgarh buried their dead in graves. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: (a) Name two materials the people of Mehrgarh used to make ornaments. (b) What kind of houses did they build?
questions.a: (a) Any two of: semi-precious stones such as lapis lazuli and carnelian, and shells. (b) Handmade sun-dried brick houses (they also built granaries).
s: (a) Any two: lapis lazuli, carnelian, shells
(b) Handmade sun-dried brick houses

questions.q: True or False: Since Mehrgarh had an agricultural village by about 7000 BCE, the whole Indian subcontinent took up farming at about that time.
questions.a: False. The chapter says there was regional variation in when agricultural ways of life began; Mehrgarh was the oldest, and only by 2500 BCE was most of the subcontinent occupied by Neolithic agricultural communities (the Sanganakallu site, for example, dates to 2000 BCE).
s: Verdict: False
Reason: regional variation; most of the subcontinent was Neolithic only by 2500 BCE (e.g. Sanganakallu, 2000 BCE)

questions.q: A student copies the crops from the chart of the transition to farming (Fig. 4.14) into her notebook as: West Asia - rice; West Africa - pearl millet; South China (Yangtze) - wheat and barley. Check each entry against the chart and correct any that are wrong.
questions.a: West Asia is wrong: the chart gives wheat and barley for West Asia. West Africa is right: pearl millet. South China (Yangtze) is wrong: the chart gives rice there.
s: West Asia wrong: wheat and barley, not rice
West Africa correct: pearl millet
South China (Yangtze) wrong: rice, not wheat and barley

questions.q: A survey team maps 50 village sites in one region of the subcontinent, all dated to about 2500 BCE. At 41 sites they find polished stone tools, pottery, the bones of cattle, sheep and goats, and grains of millets and pulses, but no metal. At the other 9 sites they find the same kind of finds together with copper objects used along with stone tools. Copper beads made at the 9 sites also turn up at several of the 41 sites. (a) Which way of life do the 41 sites show? Give two features from the finds that the chapter links to it. (b) What percentage of the 50 sites are of this kind? (c) What name does the chapter give to the culture of the 9 sites, and why? (d) A team member says, 'The two groups belong to different ages, so they could never have been in contact.' Judge this claim using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) The Neolithic agricultural way of life: cattle, sheep and goat herding along with the cultivation of cereals, millets and pulses, and polished stone tools (any two). (b) 41 / 50 = 82 per cent. (c) Chalcolithic (Copper and Stone Age), because the chapter defines it as the use of copper along with stone tools. (d) The claim does not hold: the chapter says that by 2500 BCE most of the subcontinent was occupied by Neolithic agricultural communities, sometimes interacting with the contemporary chalcolithic cultures in some parts of the country; the copper beads from the 9 sites found at the 41 sites fit such contact.
s: (a) Neolithic farming way of life, with two features (herding cattle, sheep and goats; millets and pulses; polished stone tools)
(b) 41 / 50 = 82 per cent
(c) Chalcolithic, because copper is used along with stone tools
(d) Rejects the claim: Neolithic communities sometimes interacted with contemporary chalcolithic cultures; the copper beads support contact

questions.q: Evidence of Early Harappan bead production has been found at Harappa in Pakistan, at Kunal in Haryana and at which site in Gujarat?
questions.a: Datrana

questions.q: Why is the stage before the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation generally described as 'Early Harappan'?
questions.a: because its sites show a cultural continuity into the civilisation
o: because its sites show a cultural continuity into the civilisation
because it came after the decline of the Harappan cities
because only the city of Harappa existed at that time
because its people first wrote on clay tablets with a wedge-shaped reed

questions.q: Match each Early Harappan site in Column I with the evidence the chapter links to it in Column II. Column I: 1. Bhirrana  2. Datrana  3. Kalibangan  4. Rehman Dheri. Column II: (a) a few seals with geometric and simple animal motifs  (b) radio-carbon dates suggesting the Pre-Harappan phase began between 7000 and 5500 BCE  (c) Early Harappan bead production  (d) a ploughed field with horizontal and vertical furrows
(a) Besides pottery, name two crafts that the chapter says show gradual development among the Harappans. (b) In what two ways do pottery remains from different regions show unique styles?
questions.a: (a) Any two of: copper work, shell work, the production of semi-precious stone beads. (b) In the shapes of the vessels and in their painted designs.
s: (a) Any two: copper work, shell work, semi-precious stone beads
(b) Shapes of vessels and painted designs

questions.q: In a museum, a visitor sees a pot from Kunal scratched with graffiti and a small seal from Harappa with a simple animal motif, both from the Early Harappan stage. (a) What later features of the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation does the chapter see such objects as forerunners of? (b) What do they suggest about how the Harappan script came about?
questions.a: (a) The script and the inscribed seals of the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation. (b) That the script did not appear suddenly in the cities: it probably had its beginnings in the Early Harappan stage.
s: (a) Forerunners of the Harappan script and inscribed seals
(b) The script probably began in the Early Harappan stage, not suddenly

questions.q: A poster says, 'All the Early Harappan settlements made the same kind of pottery from the start, and that is why the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation looked so uniform.' Test the claim: what the chapter says about the pottery of this stage, how the standard features of the civilisation came about, and when.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. The chapter says this was a period of large-scale production of pottery showing diverse regional styles, and pottery remains from different regions show unique styles in the shapes of vessels and their painted designs. The regional styles became more evident from 4000 BCE onwards, and many of them evolved over time and became standard features of the civilisation only by about 2500 BCE, some 1,500 years later. So the uniformity grew slowly out of regional variety; it was not there from the start.
s: Pottery of the stage showed diverse regional styles in vessel shapes and painted designs
Many regional styles evolved over time into the civilisation's standard features, by about 2500 BCE (from 4000 BCE onwards, about 1,500 years)
Verdict: claim wrong; uniformity came later out of regional variety

questions.q: A Class 9 student is writing four labels for an Early Harappan display. Write one line for each object. (a) A copper tool: what did copper tools do for the communities of the alluvial plains of the Indus and Ghaggar-Sarasvati basins? (b) A painted pot: what was the place of pottery in the Harappan economy? (c) A shell bangle: name two other items, besides shell bangles, that show continuity into the civilisation. (d) A cubical stone weight: what number pattern did the weights for smaller units follow?
questions.a: (a) They enhanced productivity, leading to increased prosperity. (b) Pottery was one of the major craft products that boosted their economy. (c) Any two of: pottery traditions, semi-precious stone beads, terracotta objects, copper working. (d) Binary multiples: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and so on.
s: (a) Copper tools enhanced productivity and prosperity
(b) Pottery was a major craft that boosted the economy
(c) Two of: pottery traditions, stone beads, terracotta objects, copper working
(d) Binary multiples 1, 2, 4, 8, 16

questions.q: 'The Early Harappan stage laid the foundation of the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation.' Evaluate this statement. (a) Give one piece of evidence from farming. (b) Give one from crafts. (c) Give one from trade and measurement. (d) Give one from seals, writing or settlement planning. (e) Point out one limit in the evidence the chapter itself signals, and give your overall verdict.
questions.a: (a) Copper tools in the fertile alluvial plains enhanced productivity, and the ploughed field at Kalibangan with horizontal and vertical furrows indicates double cropping. (b) Continuity in pottery traditions, semi-precious stone beads, shell bangles, terracotta objects and copper working. (c) A standard system of weights (binary multiples for smaller units, multiples of ten for larger ones) supported efficient interregional trade. (d) The perimeter wall around settlements, the use of seals and the script probably began in this stage; graffiti and early seals at Harappa, Rehman Dheri and Kunal are forerunners. (e) The chapter says these beginnings were 'probably' in this stage and the graffiti 'could be seen as' forerunners, so that part is not certain; still, the continuity in crafts and the gains in farming and trade are clear, and the chapter itself says these advances and economic integration led to the urban centres, so the statement is well supported.
s: (a) Farming: copper tools raised productivity, or double cropping at Kalibangan
(b) Crafts: continuity in pottery, beads, shell bangles, terracotta, copper working
(c) Standard weights supporting interregional trade
(d) Seals, script or perimeter wall probably began in this stage
(e) Notes the 'probably' limit and gives a justified verdict that the statement is well supported

questions.q: Read the statements about the city-states of Mesopotamia. Statement I: The Akkadians spoke a language different from Sumerian but used the same cuneiform script. Statement II: Assur, which took supremacy from the Akkadians, was a city-state in northern Mesopotamia. Statement III: The Assyrian civilisation lasted till early 1400 BCE. Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I and II only

questions.q: Assertion (A): The Code of Hammurabi served as a foundational model for many future legal systems. Reason (R): Hammurabi came to power in 1900 BCE, the year in which Babylonia was founded. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Name two things that, according to the chapter, the Sumerians were the first to build, use or invent.
questions.a: Any two of: a system of dams and canals for irrigation; mud bricks and burnt bricks for houses and walls; writing (cuneiform, around 3200 BCE); the wheeled cart and the sailboat.
s: First correct 'first' (dams and canals, mud and burnt bricks, writing, wheeled cart or sailboat)
A second correct 'first' from the same list

questions.q: Answer in one line each. (a) From which word does 'cuneiform' come, and what does that word mean? (b) How was cuneiform written? (c) Name two kinds of workers whose activities were recorded on the tablets.
questions.a: (a) From the Latin word cuneus, meaning 'wedge'. (b) By pressing a sharp wedge-shaped reed or stylus into the damp surface of soft clay tablets. (c) Any two of: potters, seal cutters, shipbuilders, carpenters, farm workers.
s: (a) Latin cuneus, meaning wedge
(b) Wedge-shaped reed pressed into damp clay tablets
(c) Two of: potters, seal cutters, shipbuilders, carpenters, farm workers

questions.q: A history club is making a timeline of Mesopotamia. Its cards read: Sumerian city-states from 3500 BCE; Akkad overshadows Sumer in 2334 BCE; Assur takes supremacy from Akkad around 2154 BCE; the Assyrians last till early 1700 BCE; Babylonia gains dominance from 1900 BCE; Hammurabi rises in 1792 BCE; Babylonia loses its prominence by the end of 1400 BCE. (a) Which two powers were dominant at the same time, and in which parts of Mesopotamia was each dominant? (b) For about how many years did their dominance overlap? (c) How many years after Babylonia gained dominance did Hammurabi rise, and what did he do with the small city-state? (d) The club can put only one Babylonian card under the heading 'Most lasting legacy': Hammurabi's empire or his Code. Which should it choose? Justify.
questions.a: (a) The Assyrians, dominant in the north, and the Babylonians, dominant in central Mesopotamia. (b) From 1900 BCE to early 1700 BCE: 1900 - 1700 = about 200 years. (c) 1900 - 1792 = 108 years; he conquered the neighbouring regions and expanded the small city-state into a large empire. (d) The Code: the empire lost its prominence by the end of 1400 BCE, but the Code of Hammurabi, his compilation of rules for civil and social conduct, served as a foundational model for many future legal systems.
s: (a) Assyrians in the north and Babylonians in central Mesopotamia
(b) 1900 - 1700 = about 200 years
(c) 108 years; expanded the city-state into a large empire
(d) Chooses the Code: the empire faded by 1400 BCE but the Code became a model for later legal systems

questions.q: Kabir says, 'Writing was the most important thing the Sumerians gave the world, more important than their canals, bricks or wheeled carts.' Evaluate his claim. (a) What did the Sumerian dams and canals make possible? (b) What did mud bricks and burnt bricks make possible? (c) What did the wheeled cart and the sailboat help with? (d) Give two things that writing made possible which none of these could. (e) Give your verdict on Kabir's claim with a reason.
questions.a: (a) Irrigation of fields, which supported farming, the mainstay of people's lives. (b) The building of houses, defensive walls and other structures. (c) Transport of people and goods, helping trade. (d) Any two: keeping records of farming and craft activities; preserving myths, epics, hymns, law codes and educational treatises; a common script used all over Mesopotamia by 3000 BCE by city-states speaking different languages; it gave scribes a high status. (e) A reasoned verdict, for example: Kabir is largely right, because writing preserved knowledge and allowed records and laws across city-states, and it is why the Sumerians mark the historical period; but the canals and farming produced the surplus on which cities, and so writing, depended, so writing was the most important only together with them.
s: (a) Canals and dams: irrigation that supported farming
(b) Bricks: houses, defensive walls and other structures
(c) Wheeled cart and sailboat: transport and trade
(d) Two things only writing made possible (records, literature and laws, a shared script)
(e) Verdict weighing writing against the farming base, with a reason

questions.q: In early Egypt, what was a mastaba?
questions.a: a rectangular structure placed over the burial chamber of a pharaoh
o: a rectangular structure placed over the burial chamber of a pharaoh
a tower-like stepped temple built for a city's chief god
a labelled jar in which papyrus scrolls were stored
a musical instrument played when a god's statue was paraded

questions.q: The Egyptian calendar was based on the rising of which star?

questions.q: True or False: The Egyptians cared about the soul only, so what happened to the body after death did not matter to them.
questions.a: False. The Egyptians believed each person had a ka, a spiritual double, that lived on after death only if the body was preserved. So they preserved it with great care through mummification (removing the organs except the heart, drying with natron, oiling and wrapping in linen), and the pyramids were built primarily because of this belief.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: the ka lived on only if the body was preserved, hence mummification and the pyramids

questions.q: Tara says, 'Egyptian papyrus records were only about medicine and the lives of kings.' Test her claim using what the chapter says about papyrus, libraries and stories.
questions.a: Her claim is wrong. Papyrus records preserved both stories and practical details; the Papyrus Ebers does list more than 700 cures and spells of medicine. But libraries from 2000 BCE stored papyrus scrolls in labelled jars, one holding the oldest version of 'Sindbad the Sailor', and the short stories include animal fables like 'Aesop's Fables', tales of ghosts, miracles and romances, and the oldest known form of 'Cinderella'. So papyrus covered far more than medicine and kings.
s: Medicine is present (Papyrus Ebers, 700+ cures and spells), and papyrus kept practical details
But libraries also held stories: Sindbad, animal fables, ghosts, miracles, romances, Cinderella
Verdict: claim wrong; papyrus covered far more than medicine and kings

questions.q: A school is making a timeline banner of Egyptian civilisation, with 1 cm standing for 10 years. It will run from the start of the Bronze Age in 3100 BCE to the end of the New Kingdom. Fig. 4.28 gives: Old Kingdom 2686-2181 BCE, Middle Kingdom 2030-1650 BCE, New Kingdom 1570-1069 BCE. (a) How long will the whole banner be? (b) How long will the Old Kingdom band be? (c) There is a gap between the Old and Middle Kingdoms and another between the Middle and New Kingdoms. Which gap is longer, and by how many years? (d) The designer wants to colour the longest kingdom in gold and says, 'That is the New Kingdom.' Is she right? Justify with figures.
questions.a: (a) 3100 - 1069 = 2031 years, so 2031 / 10 = 203.1 cm. (b) 2686 - 2181 = 505 years, so 50.5 cm. (c) Old to Middle: 2181 - 2030 = 151 years; Middle to New: 1650 - 1570 = 80 years; the first gap is longer, by 151 - 80 = 71 years. (d) No: the Old Kingdom lasted 505 years, the New Kingdom 1570 - 1069 = 501 years and the Middle Kingdom 2030 - 1650 = 380 years, so the Old Kingdom is the longest, though only by 4 years.
s: (a) 2031 years, banner 203.1 cm
(b) 505 years, band 50.5 cm
(c) Gaps 151 and 80 years; the first is longer by 71 years
(d) Not right: Old 505, New 501, Middle 380 years; Old Kingdom is the longest

questions.q: Neha says, 'The Han dynasty was the first imperial dynasty of China, and like the Shang it belonged to the Bronze Age.' Test both parts of her claim using the dates the chapter gives.
questions.a: Both parts are wrong. The chapter calls the Qin dynasty (221-206 BCE) the first imperial dynasty, credited with unifying the country; the Han (206 BCE-220 CE) came after the Qin. The Shang (1600-1046 BCE) was a Bronze Age dynasty, but iron had become popular throughout China by 600 BCE, so the Han, starting in 206 BCE, about 400 years later, belongs to the Iron Age, as the chapter says.
s: First imperial dynasty was the Qin (221-206 BCE), not the Han (206 BCE-220 CE)
Iron popular by 600 BCE; Han began in 206 BCE, so it was an Iron Age dynasty, unlike the Bronze Age Shang (1600-1046 BCE)
Verdict: both parts of the claim are wrong

questions.q: Compare how we know about early Mesopotamia and early China. (a) What were the main written sources of Mesopotamia, and how were they made? (b) What does the chapter call the earliest source of information about China, and how was it used? (c) What does each kind of source tell historians about the people? (d) Give one way in which China's later records differ from these earliest sources.
questions.a: (a) Cuneiform tablets, made by pressing wedge-shaped reeds into damp clay tablets. (b) The 'oracles': symbols made on pieces of animal bone and tortoise shell, which were heated until they cracked; interpretations were made from the patterns of the cracks, often to foretell the future. (c) The tablets give a glimpse of lives and beliefs (myths, epics, hymns, law codes, educational treatises) and records of farming and crafts; the oracles tell us about the hopes, desires and fears of the early Chinese. (d) China later had an abundance of historical records, because official historiographers recorded events.
s: (a) Cuneiform clay tablets pressed with wedge-shaped reeds
(b) Oracles on bone and tortoise shell, heated until cracked and read to foretell the future
(c) Tablets: lives, beliefs and records of work; oracles: hopes, desires and fears
(d) Later Chinese records kept by official historiographers

questions.q: A student writes, 'Early China grew up cut off from the rest of the world and had no outside links at all.' Evaluate the statement. (a) What does the chapter say about direct contact between China and the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation? (b) What does the chapter say about how the major Bronze Age civilisations emerged? (c) Where did the jade for Chinese ritual and prestige objects come from? (d) From which period was silk known to the Chinese, and what did it become in the Bronze Age? (e) Give your verdict on the statement with a reason.
questions.a: (a) There is little tangible evidence of direct contact between the Chinese and the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisations. (b) They emerged independently in fertile river plains and developed their social and administrative systems independently. (c) Jade was not locally available and was obtained from outside China. (d) Silk was known from the Neolithic period (4000-3000 BCE) and became an important craft during the Bronze Age. (e) The statement is only partly right: China did develop independently and had little direct contact with the Harappans, but it was not cut off, since it obtained jade from outside and later traded silk widely along the Silk Route.
s: (a) Little tangible evidence of direct contact with the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation
(b) Bronze Age civilisations emerged and organised themselves independently
(c) Jade was obtained from outside China
(d) Silk known from the Neolithic (4000-3000 BCE); an important craft in the Bronze Age
(e) Verdict: partly right; independent growth but outside links through jade and silk
